name: Tuscan Red
lede: Tuscan red is a dusky brownish red, and also a pigment name that the old colormen applied to iron-oxide reds sold with a dye lake added.

sections.title: An iron red with a dye
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium groups Tuscan red with Venetian red, Indian red, Pompeiian red, light red, rouge, Terra Pozzuoli, colcothar and caput mortuum, a family of names mostly applied to synthetic iron-oxide reds [1]. Weber, in 1923, describes red iron oxides as purer than ochres, and says Tuscan red and Pompeiian red were iron oxide mixed with alizarin madder [1]. Heaton, in 1928, said fuchsine, the aniline dye, was part of Tuscan red together with an iron oxide, as an "aniline lake such as magenta" [2].

The books therefore describe the pigment as variable: different red dyes on different iron-oxide bases, sold under one name [2]. Linked colors include [[pompeian-red]], [[venetian-red]] and [[indian-red]], and the dye side connects to [[magenta]] and the [[irresistible]] family.

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: As a color name, Tuscan red appears in several standards [3]. Our swatch is the ISCC-NBS and Werner-era dusky red, and Maerz and Paul record the name from about 1850 [3]. Our data finds a near-duplicate called Cochineal Red in Werner's list, 0.5 units apart, and Neutral Red 2.2 units apart [3]. In a modern paint chart the pigment name appears with burnt sienna, in a comparison of artists' colors by Baty [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Tuscan red is moderately common in paintings, in 205 of 23,781, more than 57 per cent of named colors [5]. It is most often an accent, in 52 per cent of the 91 paintings where it is measurable [5]. It peaks in the 1400s at 0.8 per cent of the 945 paintings we have, 1.9 times the museums' baseline [5]. The earliest match is from around 1000, centuries before the name, so it is a look-alike hue and not evidence of the pigment [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test. [5]

questions.q: According to Weber, Tuscan red was iron oxide mixed with what?
True or false: Tuscan red as a pigment name always meant one fixed recipe.

openers: Tuscan red was sold as iron oxide with a dye added: madder in one account, fuchsine in another.
